calls.reason: The June 2023 Hendrycks et al. overview sets malicious use, race dynamics and organizational failures apart from rogue AI. The Liang et al. study shows real bias harms from ordinary AI detectors. Neither pathway needs an uncontrollable superintelligence.

Turner et al. say their power-seeking results do not prove superintelligent agents will seek power. That fits uncertainty but also offers partial clues. No broad assessment settles 'haven't a clue', which is mostly rhetorical.

The forecast has no deadline. The Forecasting Research Institute study shows long-term risk forecasts can't yet be validated, but it gives neither a validated method nor an impossibility result, so the outcome isn't decided.

No survey from the period measures whether people are willing to discuss AI risk. The 2022 AI Impacts survey and Bengio's essay speak to beliefs and disagreement, not to how many refuse to talk about it.

The Forecasting Research Institute tournament shows lasting disagreement, and the one skeptical post in the packet still allows paths to catastrophe. But nothing comprehensively evaluates the arguments for negligible risk, so the universal 'no solid argument' claim can't be called.
